reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ATS-ERS
clinicalPearls: A rare cause of pulmonary hypertension in which obstruction lies in the post-capillary pulmonary venules and small veins rather than the arteries
Presents like other forms of pulmonary arterial hypertension with progressive breathlessness, fatigue, and eventual right heart failure, making it easy to misclassify
The pulmonary artery wedge pressure is characteristically normal despite the venous obstruction, because it reflects pressure upstream of the occluded venules
High-resolution CT typically shows a triad of centrilobular ground-glass opacities, smooth septal line thickening, and mediastinal lymph node enlargement
Hereditary disease is associated with biallelic mutations in the EIF2AK4 gene
It is critical to distinguish PVOD from typical pulmonary arterial hypertension, since vasodilator therapy can precipitate severe pulmonary oedema
There is no reliably effective medical therapy, and lung transplantation is the definitive treatment for eligible patients
A markedly reduced diffusing capacity with hypoxaemia out of proportion to other findings should raise suspicion
reference.pathophysiology: In pulmonary veno-occlusive disease there is widespread fibrous obliteration and remodelling of the pulmonary venules and small veins, sometimes accompanied by capillary proliferation (pulmonary capillary haemangiomatosis, now regarded as part of the same spectrum). Obstruction to venous outflow raises pressure in the upstream capillaries and pulmonary arteries, producing pre-capillary-pattern pulmonary hypertension while the left atrial and wedge pressures remain normal. Chronic capillary congestion leads to interstitial oedema, septal thickening, and occult alveolar haemorrhage. Because the arterioles remain relatively spared, pulmonary arterial vasodilators can flood the fixed downstream obstruction and cause acute pulmonary oedema.
additionalDifferentials: Pulmonary hypertension due to left heart disease
Interstitial lung disease with secondary pulmonary hypertension
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution CT of the chest for the characteristic triad of findings
Right heart catheterisation demonstrating pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension with a normal wedge pressure
Pulmonary function testing with a disproportionately reduced diffusing capacity
Genetic testing for EIF2AK4 mutations in suspected hereditary or familial cases
Echocardiography to assess right heart size and function
Assessment for associated conditions and transplant eligibility
redFlags: Acute pulmonary oedema following initiation of pulmonary vasodilator therapy - a recognised emergency in this disease
Rapidly worsening breathlessness and hypoxaemia signalling clinical deterioration
Signs of decompensated right heart failure such as syncope, hypotension, or rising oxygen requirement
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is poor with a rapidly progressive course, limited response to medical therapy, and high mortality; lung transplantation offers the only definitive treatment and referral should be early.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as ordinary pulmonary arterial hypertension and starting vasodilators that precipitate pulmonary oedema
Overlooking the diagnosis when the wedge pressure is normal despite congestive imaging findings
Delaying transplant referral given the aggressive course
Failing to recognise the characteristic CT triad
management: Refer early for lung transplantation, the only definitive treatment, given the poor and rapidly progressive course
Avoid or use targeted pulmonary arterial vasodilators only with extreme caution in an expert centre, as they can precipitate severe pulmonary oedema
Provide supportive supplemental oxygen for hypoxaemia and cautious diuretic therapy for pulmonary congestion
Offer EIF2AK4 genetic testing and cascade family counselling where hereditary disease is suspected
Manage exclusively within a specialist pulmonary hypertension centre with facilities for close monitoring
Support with immunisation and advise on avoidance of pregnancy and other high-risk states
Monitor right ventricular function and oxygenation closely, escalating promptly on deterioration
